title: What healthy training looks like
summary: Learn the vital signs of a GRPO run: reward, reward spread and all-same groups, completion length, KL, entropy and clip ratio. See what each measures, what a healthy shape looks like, and which curves to read together.
learningObjectives: Explain in plain words what each main GRPO metric in TRL measures
Describe the healthy shape of reward, length, KL, entropy, clip ratio and frac_reward_zero_std
Read curves together, using rolling averages, instead of judging one number
Explain why held-out accuracy must be checked alongside training reward

studyGuide.mentalModel: A doctor's chart. Reward is the headline, but it can lie on its own. Held-out accuracy confirms it, the fraction of all-same groups is the fuel gauge, length is the thinking budget, KL is distance from home, entropy is confidence, and clip ratio says how hard the brake is working. Health is when they tell the same story.
keyIdeas: With small batches every point is noisy; read rolling averages and trends over tens of steps.
Healthy reward rises then flattens, and held-out accuracy rises with it.
frac_reward_zero_std near 1 means almost no learning signal; DAPO's dynamic sampling filters such groups.
Healthy entropy declines gently while reward rises; a sharp drop with flat reward is collapse.
With num_iterations = 1, clip ratio near zero is expected; KL should rise slowly and smoothly.
misconceptions: A rising reward alone does not prove the model learned the task.
Falling entropy is not automatically bad; it is healthy when the model is becoming confidently right.
A clip ratio of zero is not a bug when TRL does one update per batch.
Longer answers are not automatically better reasoning; check accuracy and the cut-off share.
recallPrompts: Which TRL metric tells you the share of groups that teach nothing?
What does healthy entropy look like, and what curve do you check alongside it?
Why is clip ratio near zero in a default TRL GRPO run?
What should you check when completion length keeps rising?
studyGuide.explainBackPrompt: Explain to a friend why you would never judge a training run by its reward curve alone, using two other curves as examples.

quiz.prompt: frac_reward_zero_std sits near 0.95 for the whole run. What does that tell you?
options: The run is extremely healthy
Almost every group has all answers scoring the same, so there is almost no learning signal
The KL penalty is too low
The model is writing very long answers
quiz.explanation: All-same groups have zero advantage. At 0.95, 95% of groups teach nothing: the data is too hard or too easy for the model, or groups are too small.

options: Entropy falls sharply in the first 20 steps while reward stays flat
Entropy rises steadily while reward falls
Entropy declines gently while reward and held-out accuracy rise
Entropy stays exactly constant and reward stays exactly constant
quiz.explanation: Gentle decline with rising reward means the model is becoming confident because it is right. A sharp drop with flat reward is collapse; rising entropy often means garbled text.

quiz.prompt: Your TRL run uses the default num_iterations = 1 and clip_ratio/region_mean is about 0 throughout. What should you do?
options: Nothing: with one update per batch the ratio is about 1, so clipping rarely triggers
Stop the run, clipping is broken
Raise epsilon to 10
Set beta to 1.0
quiz.explanation: Clipping only acts when the policy has moved since sampling, which needs more than one update per batch.

quiz.prompt: Why does the notebook draw a rolling average over the reward curve?
options: Because TRL logs rewards in the wrong units
To hide bad results
Because rolling averages make training faster
Because each step uses very few questions, so single points are noisy and the trend is what matters
quiz.explanation: With 2 questions per step, one easy or hard question swings the value. The rolling average shows the underlying trend.

quiz.prompt: Completion length rises steadily and completions/clipped_ratio climbs toward 0.5, but held-out accuracy is flat. What is the best reading?
options: Healthy: longer answers always mean better reasoning
The KL is too low
Suspicious: answers are growing and being cut off without any accuracy gain, so the model may be rambling
The learning rate is too low
quiz.explanation: Length growth is healthy only alongside accuracy gains. Half the answers hitting the limit means they are cut off mid-thought; see the next lesson for fixes.

interactive.caption: Start with the healthy preset: notice the flat start, reward and accuracy rising together, and entropy falling as accuracy rises. Then compare with hacking, stuck and tight leash.
